title: SQL injection in product search
description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the untrusted 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the URL-encoded query string.
evidence: Code path: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1 -- . Against running app: request to /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all 6 products instead of zero matches.

title: SQL injection in admin reviews report
description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint uses Python f-string interpolation to embed customer.display_name directly into SQL. Any user whose display_name contains SQL metacharacters can trigger injection when a staff member queries reviews for that customer.
evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC". Display name is user-controlled at registration time.

title: IDOR on order detail endpoint allows viewing other users' orders
description: The GET /orders/<order_id> endpoint delegates to get_order() which only checks whether the order exists. It does not verify that the requesting user owns the order. Any authenticated user can view another user's order details including refund history.
evidence: Confirmed interactively: logged in as priya.shah@mail.test (customer_id=1) and successfully retrieved order 3, which belongs to tom.okafor@mail.test (customer_id=2).

title: Arbitrary code execution via pickle deserialization in basket cookie
description: The basket cookie value is decoded from base64 and passed directly to pickle.loads(). Because the cookie is settable by the browser and stored client-side, an attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code when deserialized by the server.
evidence: Line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Pickle is inherently unsafe for untrusted data; any user can craft or modify the basket cookie.

title: JWT signature verification disabled in token refresh
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False. An attacker can forge a JWT with any 'sub' claim (user ID), including any admin/staff user, and obtain a valid signed token — effectively hijacking any account without knowing the signing key.
evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}). Confirmed by inspecting source; the refresh flow accepts a forged token as proof of identity.

title: Predictable password-reset tokens
description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8), using Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded with system time. With ~2^27 possible values and deterministic seeding, tokens are trivially guessable, enabling brute-force password resets.
evidence: Line 135: token = "%08d" % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 8-digit numeric codes (00000000–99999999), plus random.seed() defaults to time-based seed.

title: Password hashing without salt
description: Passwords are hashed with plain SHA-256 and no salt. Identical passwords produce identical hashes, making rainbow-table attacks effective. Salt + iterative hashing (e.g., bcrypt, argon2) is required.
evidence: Line 16: hash_password(password) returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Seed script confirms all demo accounts use the same password hash.

title: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY
description: The Flask SECRET_KEY is baked into the source file. Anyone with read access to the repo knows the session signing key, allowing forging of session cookies and JWT tokens if the signing algorithm is compromised.
evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". Used for both Flask sessions and JWT HS256 signing.

title: Weak and known WEBHOOK_SECRET default
description: The webhook secret falls back to the hardcoded string 'whsec-local'. Anyone who reads the source code can forge valid payment webhooks, potentially changing order statuses fraudulently.
evidence: Line 8: WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get("WEBHOOK_SECRET", "whsec-local"). Webhook handler trusts its HMAC signature blindly.

title: Overly permissive CORS configuration
description: The CORS handler reflects the Origin header back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Allow-Credentials: true. Combined with wildcard-origin-like behavior, this means any website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the API.
evidence: Lines 44-51: resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin, combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True. For any origin X, browser will send cookies with cross-origin requests.

title: Sensitive data logged in request body
description: All POST, PUT, and PATCH request bodies are written to the log file (up to 2000 bytes). Login attempts, registration, and password-reset requests may contain plaintext passwords or PII.
evidence: Line 31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Affects /auth/login, /auth/register, /auth/reset/request.
